lessons.title: Why Financial Literacy Matters
lessons.conceptMarkdown:
## Why This Matters

Money isn't just numbers — it's a tool for buying *time*, *options*, and *security*. People who understand a few core concepts (budgeting, saving, compound interest) consistently make better long-term decisions than those who don't, regardless of how much they earn.

This course won't tell you what stocks to buy or make you rich overnight. It teaches the fundamentals: how to control your spending, build a safety net, and understand how money grows over time.

**This is educational content, not financial advice.**

questions.prompt: What is the main goal of this course?

options.label: To teach core financial concepts and habits
To give you specific stock picks
To guarantee you get rich quickly

questions.prompt: True or false: understanding money matters even if you don't earn a lot.

lessons.title: Setting a Financial Goal
lessons.conceptMarkdown:
## Setting a Financial Goal

A goal without a number and a date is just a wish. Compare:

- ❌ "I want to save more money."
- ✅ "I want to save $1,000 for an emergency fund in the next 6 months."

Good financial goals are **specific** (a clear target), **measurable** (a number), and **time-bound** (a deadline). This makes it possible to track progress and know when you've actually succeeded.

questions.prompt: Which of these is the BEST example of a specific financial goal?

options.label: Save $1,000 for an emergency fund in 6 months
Try to save some money this year

questions.prompt: A good financial goal should be specific, measurable, and...

lessons.title: Income vs. Expenses
lessons.conceptMarkdown:
## Income vs. Expenses

Every budget starts with one equation:

**Income − Expenses = Surplus (or Deficit)**

- **Income** is money coming in: salary, side gigs, gifts.
- **Expenses** are money going out: rent, food, subscriptions.

If you spend less than you earn, you have a **surplus** — money you can save or invest. If you spend more than you earn, you have a **deficit**, and the gap usually goes on a credit card, which makes next month harder.

A budget is simply a *plan* for this equation, made *before* the month starts instead of discovering the result after.

questions.prompt: You earn $3,000 a month and spend $3,200. You have a...
What is a budget, most simply?

options.label: A plan for your income and expenses made in advance

lessons.title: The 50/30/20 Rule
lessons.conceptMarkdown:
## The 50/30/20 Rule

A simple starting budget for your *take-home pay* (what actually hits your bank account after taxes):

- **50% Needs** — rent, groceries, utilities, insurance, minimum debt payments
- **30% Wants** — dining out, streaming, hobbies, travel
- **20% Savings & extra debt payoff** — emergency fund, investing, extra payments

The exact split doesn't matter; the *habit* does. If 50/30/20 doesn't fit your city's rent, try 60/20/20 — just keep savings above zero.

**Pro tip:** move savings out on payday, not at month's end. What's left over tends to vanish; what's moved first tends to stick.

questions.prompt: In the 50/30/20 rule, what does the 20% represent?
Why save money on payday instead of at the end of the month?

options.label: Money moved first tends to stay saved; leftovers tend to get spent
Banks only accept deposits on payday
It earns double interest that way

lessons.title: Needs vs. Wants
lessons.conceptMarkdown:
## Needs vs. Wants

- **Needs** keep you housed, fed, and employable: rent, groceries, basic clothes, insurance, minimum debt payments.
- **Wants** make life enjoyable: restaurants, games, concerts, a nicer phone.

The test is *situational*, not moral. Food is a need; a $60 dinner is a want. A phone may be a need for your job; the latest flagship model is a want.

Wants aren't bad — a budget with zero fun almost never survives. The goal is to **choose** your wants deliberately instead of discovering them on your credit card statement.

questions.prompt: Which of these is clearly a NEED?
The needs-vs-wants test is best described as...

options.label: Situational — it depends on your circumstances
Fixed — the same items for everyone, always

lessons.title: Spotting Leaks
lessons.conceptMarkdown:
## Spotting Leaks

Small recurring charges drain serious money:

- A $12 subscription is **$144 a year**.
- Three forgotten subscriptions at $15 each are **$540 a year**.

**How to find your leaks:**

1. Pull last month's bank and card statements.
2. Highlight every recurring charge.
3. For each one ask: *"Would I sign up for this again today at 12× the price?"*
4. Cancel the ones that fail the test — ruthlessly. You can always re-subscribe.

Most people find $50–$200/month of spending they don't miss once it's gone. That's the cheapest raise you'll ever get.

questions.prompt: A $12/month subscription costs how much per year?
What's the best question to ask about a recurring charge?

options.label: "Would I sign up for this again today at 12× the price?"
"Did I use it at least once?"
"Is it cheaper than my other subscriptions?"

lessons.title: Why You Need One
lessons.conceptMarkdown:
## Why You Need One

Life throws surprises: a car repair, a medical bill, a layoff. Without savings, every surprise goes on a credit card — and debt at 20%+ interest turns one bad week into months of expensive payments. That's the **debt spiral**.

An **emergency fund** is cash reserved *only* for genuine emergencies:

- ✅ Car breaks down, job loss, surprise medical bill
- ❌ A sale on flights, a new phone, concert tickets

It's the difference between "annoying" and "disaster." A $1,000 surprise with no savings is a crisis; with savings it's a Tuesday.

questions.prompt: The main purpose of an emergency fund is to...

options.label: Cover genuine surprises without going into debt
Invest in the stock market safely

questions.prompt: Which of these is a proper emergency-fund use?

lessons.title: How Much Is Enough
lessons.conceptMarkdown:
## How Much Is Enough

Two targets, in order:

1. **Starter fund: $500–$1,000.** Small, fast to reach, covers most common surprises (tire, copay, small repair).
2. **Full fund: 3–6 months of *essential* expenses.** Rent, food, utilities, minimum payments — not your full lifestyle. This is what protects you from a job loss.

**Where to keep it:** a high-yield savings account (HYSA). It must be:

- **Liquid** — accessible within a day or two
- **Boring** — not stocks; you can't afford a 30% drop the week you need it
- **Separate** — a different account, so it doesn't get spent casually

questions.prompt: A full emergency fund typically covers how many months of ESSENTIAL expenses?
Where should an emergency fund live?

options.label: A high-yield savings account, separate from spending money
Your checking account, mixed with daily spending

lessons.title: Good vs. Bad Debt
lessons.conceptMarkdown:
## Good vs. Bad Debt

Debt isn't automatically evil — the question is *what the borrowed money buys*:

- **Potentially good:** debt that buys an appreciating asset or earning power — a mortgage on a reasonable home, a student loan for a degree with real job prospects, a business loan for a proven plan.
- **Usually bad:** debt that funds consumption — credit card balances on dinners out, financing a vacation, payday loans for everyday bills.

Two rules of thumb:

1. Borrow for things that *outlast the loan*.
2. Never borrow at high interest for something that loses value (or is gone immediately).

questions.prompt: Which is the BEST example of potentially good debt?

options.label: A student loan for a degree with strong job prospects
A credit card balance from a vacation
A payday loan to cover this month's bills

questions.prompt: The key question for judging debt is...

options.label: What does the borrowed money actually buy?
Is the lender a big bank?
Did a friend also take this loan?

lessons.title: APR Basics
lessons.conceptMarkdown:
## APR Basics

**APR (Annual Percentage Rate)** is the yearly cost of borrowing, as a percentage. A $1,000 balance at 24% APR costs about **$240/year** in interest.

Typical APR ranges:

- Payday loans: **300%+** (a $500 two-week loan can cost $75+ in fees)
- Credit cards: **20–30%**
- Auto loans: **5–10%**
- Mortgages: **3–7%**

**The minimum-payment trap:** card minimums are set barely above interest. Pay only the minimum on $3,000 at 24% and you'll spend *years* paying it off — mostly interest. Always pay more than the minimum, and treat high-APR balances as your top priority after the starter emergency fund.

questions.prompt: Roughly how much interest per year does a $1,000 balance at 24% APR cost?
Why are payday loans considered dangerous?

options.label: They require collateral like your house
They are always for larger amounts than credit cards

lessons.title: What Affects Your Score
lessons.conceptMarkdown:
## What Affects Your Score

A credit score is a number (300–850) predicting how reliably you repay. The big factors:

- **Payment history (~35%)** — the single biggest one. One missed payment can hurt for years.
- **Credit utilization (~30%)** — how much of your limit you use. Keep it **under 30%**, lower is better.
- **Length of history (~15%)** — older accounts help; don't close your oldest card without reason.
- **New credit (~10%)** — a burst of applications dings your score short-term.
- **Credit mix (~10%)** — variety helps slightly; don't force it.

**The two levers that matter most:** pay every bill on time, and keep balances low relative to limits.

questions.prompt: Which factor has the BIGGEST impact on a typical credit score?
As a rule of thumb, keep credit card utilization below...

lessons.title: Why It Matters
lessons.conceptMarkdown:
## Why It Matters

Your score follows you into more places than you'd expect:

- **Loans & cards:** a strong score can mean a mortgage at 6% instead of 8% — on a $300,000 loan, that's **tens of thousands of dollars**.
- **Renting:** landlords often check credit; a weak score can mean a bigger deposit or a rejection.
- **Insurance & utilities:** many set prices or deposits partly on credit.
- **Jobs:** some employers check credit reports (not scores) for financial roles.

**The cheapest way to protect it:** automate at least the minimum payments on every account. On-time history builds itself; one missed payment undoes months of good behavior.

questions.prompt: On a large mortgage, a better credit score can save you...

options.label: Tens of thousands of dollars in interest
Nothing — rates are fixed for everyone

questions.prompt: What's the cheapest way to protect your credit score?

options.label: Automate at least minimum payments on every account
Apply for new credit often to show activity

lessons.title: Avalanche vs. Snowball
lessons.conceptMarkdown:
## Avalanche vs. Snowball

Two proven methods, one shared rule: pay the **minimum on every debt**, then throw every extra dollar at **one target**.

- **Avalanche:** attack the **highest APR** first. Mathematically optimal — you pay the least total interest.
- **Snowball:** attack the **smallest balance** first. Quick wins build momentum and motivation.

Avalanche saves the most money; snowball keeps the most people going. **The best method is the one you'll actually finish** — follow-through matters more than interest-rate math.

questions.prompt: Which debt-payoff method targets the highest APR balance first?
The most important factor in choosing a payoff method is...

options.label: Whether you'll stick with it until the debts are gone

lessons.title: Getting Out Faster
lessons.conceptMarkdown:
## Getting Out Faster

Free up extra money for the target debt:

1. Cancel subscription leaks (Unit 3).
2. Redirect windfalls — tax refunds, bonuses, gifts — straight to debt.
3. Sell things you no longer use.

**Watch the traps:**

- A 0% balance-transfer card can help, but the intro rate **expires** (then the APR jumps) and the transfer fee is 3–5%.
- Extra payments must go to **principal**, not future interest.
- Don't close your oldest cards after paying them off — that shortens your credit history (Unit 6).

questions.prompt: A 0% balance-transfer card becomes a trap when...

options.label: The intro rate expires and the APR jumps
It's used to pay off a payday loan
The credit limit is too high

questions.prompt: After paying off a credit card, you should generally...

options.label: Keep it open to preserve your credit history

lessons.title: Checking vs. Savings
lessons.conceptMarkdown:
## Checking vs. Savings

- **Checking** — the spending account: debit card, bill pay, ATM access. Earns almost no interest, and that's fine — its job is *flow*.
- **Savings** — the parking account: money you're not spending soon. Its job is *growth* — and a **high-yield savings account (HYSA)** pays ~4% vs. ~0.01% at big traditional banks.

Both are **FDIC insured up to $250,000** per depositor per bank — the safest place money can live.

**Rule of thumb:** checking holds this month's money; savings holds everything else.

questions.prompt: Which account is designed for daily spending and bills?
Why keep savings in an HYSA instead of a big-bank savings account?

options.label: HYSAs pay ~4% vs. ~0.01% — hundreds of times more interest

lessons.title: Fees to Avoid
lessons.conceptMarkdown:
## Fees to Avoid

Bank fees are pure loss — and almost all avoidable:

- **Monthly maintenance fees** ($5–15) — usually waived with direct deposit or a minimum balance; if not, switch banks.
- **Overdraft fees** (~$35) — decline the "courtesy" overdraft so cards simply get declined instead.
- **Out-of-network ATM fees** ($3–5 each) — use in-network ATMs or a bank that rebates fees.
- **Foreign transaction fees** (1–3%) — pick a no-FX-fee card for travel.

A good bank today: **no monthly fee, no minimum, big ATM network**. Online banks check all three boxes.

questions.prompt: The most reliably avoidable bank fee is...

options.label: The monthly maintenance fee — switch banks or meet the waiver

questions.prompt: If you opt out of overdraft "protection," a purchase you can't afford will...

options.label: Be declined — usually the better outcome

lessons.title: The Eighth Wonder
lessons.conceptMarkdown:
## The Eighth Wonder

**Compound interest** means earning returns on your returns:

- Year 1: $100 grows 7% → $107
- Year 2: the *whole* $107 grows → $114.49
- Year 10: → ~$197. Year 20: → ~$387. Year 30: → ~$761

**The Rule of 72:** divide 72 by your annual return to estimate doubling time. At 7%, money doubles roughly every **10 years**.

The same force runs in reverse on debt: a credit-card balance at 24% APR doubles in about **3 years** if untouched. Compounding is the strongest force in personal finance — make sure it works *for* you.

questions.prompt: Using the Rule of 72, money invested at 8% doubles roughly every...
Compound interest works AGAINST you when you...

lessons.title: Time Is the Multiplier
lessons.conceptMarkdown:
## Time Is the Multiplier

Two people invest $200/month at a 7% average return until age 65:

- **Starts at 25:** contributes $96,000 → ends with **~$525,000**
- **Starts at 35:** contributes $72,000 → ends with **~$244,000**

The 10-year head start more than *doubles* the final result — the early dollars do the heaviest lifting because they compound longest.

**The takeaway:** you can't get time back. The most valuable thing a young investor has is *years* — and the second-best day to start is today.

questions.prompt: Two people save $200/month at 7% until 65 — one from age 25, one from 35. Who ends with more?

options.label: The one who started at 25 — by more than double
The one who started at 35 — bigger contributions

questions.prompt: The most powerful input to compound growth is...

lessons.title: Why Cash Loses Value
lessons.conceptMarkdown:
## Why Cash Loses Value

**Inflation** means prices rise over time — each dollar buys a little less every year. US inflation has averaged ~3% annually: at that pace, $100 buys about **$97** of goods next year and ~$74 in ten years.

That's why the mattress is the riskiest place for long-term money: it's *guaranteed* to lose purchasing power.

**Real return** is what's left after inflation:

> Real return = Nominal return − Inflation

A savings account paying 1% with 3% inflation has a **−2% real return** — a slow, silent loss.

questions.prompt: Real return is calculated as...
Your savings pay 1% while inflation runs 3%. Your real return is...

lessons.title: Beating Inflation
lessons.conceptMarkdown:
## Beating Inflation

To *grow* purchasing power, your after-fee, after-tax return must beat inflation:

- **Cash / checking (0–1%):** loses to inflation, always
- **HYSAs (~4%):** usually keeps pace
- **Stocks (~10% nominal / ~7% real long-run average):** historically the reliable long-term winner

This is why long-horizon money gets **invested**, not saved — investing isn't about getting rich; it's about not getting poorer.

**The exception:** your emergency fund. Its job is instant access and zero risk, not growth — a small real loss is the fair price of that safety.

questions.prompt: Over the long run, which has most reliably beaten inflation?
Why doesn't the emergency fund need to beat inflation?

options.label: Its job is instant access and safety, not growth

lessons.title: Stocks, Bonds, Funds
lessons.conceptMarkdown:
## Stocks, Bonds, Funds

The three building blocks:

- **Stock** — a tiny ownership slice of a company. Returns come from growth and dividends; prices swing hard.
- **Bond** — a *loan* to a company or government. It pays fixed interest and ranks ahead of stockholders if things go wrong: steadier, lower returns.
- **Fund (ETF / mutual fund)** — a basket of hundreds of stocks and/or bonds in one purchase: instant diversification.

**Risk ↔ return:** higher potential return always comes with higher potential loss. There is no high-return, no-risk asset — anyone promising one is selling something else.

questions.prompt: Owning one share of stock means you...

options.label: Own a small piece of that company

questions.prompt: Compared to a single stock, a fund is...

options.label: Less risky because it spreads money across many holdings
More risky because it holds more things

lessons.title: Risk vs. Return
lessons.conceptMarkdown:
## Risk vs. Return

The risk ladder (long-run averages, not promises):

- **Savings / HYSAs:** 0–4%, essentially no risk (FDIC)
- **Bonds:** 2–5%, mild swings
- **Stocks:** ~7–10% average, with years of −30%+ on the way

**Your time horizon picks your rung.** Money you need within ~3–5 years (emergency fund, next year's tuition, a down payment) doesn't belong in stocks — a bad year right before you need it is a loss you can't wait out. Long-horizon money (retirement) can ride out the swings and should take the growth.

questions.prompt: Money you need for a down payment next year should be...

options.label: In safe, liquid accounts — not stocks

questions.prompt: "Higher expected return" in investing always comes with...

lessons.title: Why Index Funds
lessons.conceptMarkdown:
## Why Index Funds

An **index fund** doesn't try to pick winners — it just owns the whole market (e.g., all 500 S&P 500 companies). You get average market returns, which beat most professionals:

- **Low fees:** ~0.03–0.2% per year vs. 1%+ for many actively managed funds
- **Better odds:** over 15+ years, roughly 90% of active funds underperform their index
- **Zero skill required:** no research, no timing, no stock-picking luck needed

Fees compound *against* you exactly like returns compound for you: 1% extra in fees over 30 years can eat **a quarter or more** of your final balance.

questions.prompt: An S&P 500 index fund holds...

options.label: All (or most) of the 500 largest US companies
Only companies that beat the market

questions.prompt: Why do fund fees matter so much?

options.label: They compound against you every single year

lessons.title: Don't Pick Stocks
lessons.conceptMarkdown:
## Don't Pick Stocks

Picking stocks that beat the market, consistently, is nearly impossible — most professionals fail at it, and one company can go to **zero** (Enron, Lehman) while the market as a whole has always recovered.

**Time in the market beats timing the market.** Missing just the 10 best days over a few decades can cut your total return roughly in half — and the best days cluster right after the worst ones, exactly when selling feels safest.

The whole strategy in one sentence: **buy a total-market index fund, automatically, every month, for decades, and ignore the noise.**

questions.prompt: "Time in the market beats timing the market" means...

options.label: Staying invested long-term beats trying to buy and sell at perfect moments
Day trading is the fastest path to wealth
Wait for a crash before investing

questions.prompt: The key danger of holding a single company's stock is...

options.label: One company can fail while the whole market recovers

lessons.title: Tax-Advantaged Accounts
lessons.conceptMarkdown:
## Tax-Advantaged Accounts

Retirement accounts (401(k), IRA, or your country's equivalents) are special wrappers around the same index funds — with a superpower: **investments inside them compound without yearly tax drag.**

- **Traditional:** contributions reduce taxable income *now*; withdrawals are taxed later.
- **Roth:** contributions are taxed *now*; qualified withdrawals are **tax-free forever**.

Either way, decades of untaxed compounding is the single biggest legal boost available to a normal investor.

The trade-offs: annual contribution limits, and withdrawals before retirement age usually owe penalties (with exceptions).

questions.prompt: The key benefit of investing inside a retirement account is...

options.label: Decades of compounding without yearly tax drag

questions.prompt: With a Roth-style account, taxes are paid...

options.label: Now — and qualified withdrawals come out tax-free

lessons.title: The Employer Match
lessons.conceptMarkdown:
## The Employer Match

Many employers match 401(k) contributions — e.g., **50 cents per dollar up to 6% of salary**. That match is an **instant 50% return** on every matched dollar. Nothing else in investing reliably offers that.

**Priority order for each paycheck:**

1. Capture the **full employer match** (free money first)
2. Kill **high-interest debt** (24% APR beats 7% returns)
3. Fill retirement accounts
4. Taxable investing / other goals

Leaving a match unclaimed is declining part of your own salary — it's the most expensive mistake in personal finance.

questions.prompt: A 50% match on contributions is effectively...

options.label: An instant 50% return on matched money

questions.prompt: Why capture the full match before other investing?

options.label: No other investment reliably returns 50% instantly

lessons.title: How Income Is Taxed
lessons.conceptMarkdown:
## How Income Is Taxed

Tax brackets are **marginal**: each slice of income is taxed at its own rate — moving into a higher bracket only taxes the *extra* dollars at the higher rate, never your whole income.

Example (simplified): if 10% applies to your first $11,000 and 12% above it, a raise from $11,000 to $12,000 pays 12% only on the last $1,000.

**Take-home pay** = gross − federal/state income tax − payroll tax (FICA ~7.65%) − pre-tax deductions. Budget from take-home, never gross — and know your **effective rate** (total tax ÷ total income), which is always lower than your top bracket.

questions.prompt: You move into a higher tax bracket. What happens?

options.label: Only the income above the threshold is taxed at the higher rate
All your income is taxed at the higher rate
You owe back taxes on prior years

questions.prompt: Your effective tax rate is...

options.label: The rate of your top bracket

lessons.title: Keeping More of Your Pay
lessons.conceptMarkdown:
## Keeping More of Your Pay

Legal ways to lower the bill:

- **Pre-tax deductions** (traditional 401(k), HSA, some insurance premiums) shrink taxable income while building wealth.
- **Credits beat deductions:** a **credit** cuts tax owed dollar-for-dollar; a **deduction** only removes taxable income. A $1,000 credit saves $1,000; a $1,000 deduction saves maybe $220.
- **A huge refund every year** means you over-withheld — an interest-free loan to the government. Adjust your withholding and put the difference to work monthly instead.

questions.prompt: Which reduces your tax bill dollar-for-dollar?
A big tax refund every year usually means...

options.label: You over-withheld — an interest-free loan to the government

lessons.title: What Insurance Actually Is
lessons.conceptMarkdown:
## What Insurance Actually Is

Insurance is **risk transfer**: thousands of people pay small premiums so that the unlucky few aren't financially destroyed. You're not betting on disaster — you're buying protection from the *catastrophic* version of it.

- **Premium:** what you pay (monthly/yearly)
- **Deductible:** what you pay out of pocket before coverage kicks in

**The rule:** insure what you *can't afford* to lose (health disaster, house fire, liability lawsuit); self-insure the small stuff (phone screens, minor repairs) with your emergency fund. Extended warranties on gadgets are usually insurance you don't need, at a price that's pure profit for the seller.

questions.prompt: The core purpose of insurance is to...

options.label: Transfer the cost of rare, unaffordable disasters

questions.prompt: A deductible is...

options.label: What you pay out of pocket before coverage starts

lessons.title: Coverage You Probably Need
lessons.conceptMarkdown:
## Coverage You Probably Need

- **Health** — the #1 cause of US bankruptcies; even a basic plan caps catastrophe.
- **Auto liability** — legally required, and one at-fault crash can dwarf any premium.
- **Renters** — ~$15/month, covers your belongings *and* liability if someone is injured in your place.
- **Term life** — if anyone depends on your income: ~10–12× your salary, for a fraction of what whole life costs.
- **Disability** — protects your *paycheck*, your biggest asset.

**Usually skip:** extended warranties, flight insurance, and whole-life policies sold as "investments" — high fees wrapped in insurance you don't need.

questions.prompt: Who most needs term life insurance?

options.label: People whose dependents rely on their income

questions.prompt: Which is usually NOT worth the price?

lessons.title: Buying a Car
lessons.conceptMarkdown:
## Buying a Car

New cars lose roughly **20% of their value in the first year** and about half within five. The cheapest move: buy **reliable used (2–3 years old)** and let the first owner absorb the steepest depreciation.

Budget the **total cost of ownership**, not the payment: insurance, fuel, maintenance, registration, and loan interest.

A common affordability guideline — the **20/4/10 rule**: at least 20% down, a loan no longer than 4 years, and total car costs under ~10% of take-home pay. A longer loan lowers the payment but often leaves you owing more than the car is worth.

questions.prompt: A new car typically loses about what share of its value in the first year?
The 20/4/10 guideline suggests...

options.label: 20% down, ≤4-year loan, car costs ≤10% of take-home pay

lessons.title: Rent vs. Buy
lessons.conceptMarkdown:
## Rent vs. Buy

**Renting is not wasted money.** It buys flexibility, zero maintenance risk, and freedom to relocate — often the right call for anyone who might move within ~5 years.

Buying makes sense when you'll **stay 5+ years**, have stable income, a full emergency fund, and a total cost (mortgage + property tax + insurance + maintenance) that fits comfortably. Beyond the mortgage, budget maintenance at roughly **1–2% of the home's value per year**, on top of property taxes and insurance.

A home is a *leveraged, illiquid, concentrated* bet on one property in one neighborhood. Buy it for stability and life fit — not as a guaranteed investment.

questions.prompt: Renting is often the right call when...

options.label: You might move within about five years

questions.prompt: Beyond the mortgage, yearly maintenance alone typically costs about what % of a home's value?

lessons.title: Raising Your Income
lessons.conceptMarkdown:
## Raising Your Income

Cutting expenses has a floor; income doesn't. The highest-ROI moves, in order:

1. **Negotiate your salary** — one conversation raises the base for *every* future raise and bonus.
2. **Switch employers** — job-switchers often land +10–20% vs. ~3–4% for those who stay.
3. **Build in-demand skills** — the market pays for scarce abilities.
4. **Side income** — freelance what you already do; watch for **self-employment tax** (set aside ~25–30% of profit).

A $5,000 raise negotiated once at 25 compounds through every subsequent raise — the same math as Unit 9, applied to your paycheck.

questions.prompt: Why is salary negotiation such a high-ROI move?

options.label: One conversation raises the base for every future raise

questions.prompt: Side income usually triggers...

options.label: Self-employment tax — set aside ~25–30% of profit

lessons.title: How to Negotiate
lessons.conceptMarkdown:
## How to Negotiate

1. **Research market rates** for your role, level, and city — you can't ask for a number you've never seen.
2. **Let them anchor first** when possible; if forced to name a number, give a range whose *bottom* you'd happily accept.
3. **Negotiate total compensation:** base, bonus, equity, PTO, remote days, start date.
4. **Practice out loud** — the words get easier.
5. **Use silence** after an offer; and always **get it in writing**.

Worst case, they say no and you've lost nothing. Most people never ask — which is exactly why asking works.

questions.prompt: The most important prep before negotiating is...

options.label: Researching market rates for your role

questions.prompt: If base salary is truly fixed, you should...

options.label: Negotiate the rest — bonus, equity, PTO, remote flexibility

lessons.title: Red Flags
lessons.conceptMarkdown:
## Red Flags

Almost every scam shares the same three ingredients:

1. **Urgency** — "act now or lose out"
2. **Secrecy** — "don't tell anyone / this is between us"
3. **Unusual payment** — gift cards, wire transfers, crypto, payment apps

See all three? It's a scam — no exceptions. Also automatic scams: "guaranteed returns," "risk-free," and anyone asking for your **password, full SSN, or a 2FA code**. Real banks and agencies never ask for those by phone, text, or email.

**If it sounds too good to be true, it is — and someone wants it to sound exactly that good.**

questions.prompt: The classic scam payment methods are...
A caller claiming to be your bank asks for the 2FA code they just "sent you." You should...

options.label: Refuse and hang up — banks never ask for it
Read it to them to be helpful

lessons.title: Protecting Yourself
lessons.conceptMarkdown:
## Protecting Yourself

- **Verify independently.** Look up the official number yourself; never use the link or number in the message.
- **Slow down.** Urgency is the scammer's main tool; legitimacy survives a night's sleep.
- **Harden accounts:** unique passwords + 2FA everywhere; monitor statements monthly.
- **Freeze your credit** (free at all three US bureaus) if you fear identity theft — it blocks new accounts in your name without affecting your score.
- **If hit:** contact your bank immediately, report to the FTC (US) or your local equivalent, and freeze credit the same day.

Scammers hunt the rushed, the trusting, and the hopeful. Be none of the three.

questions.prompt: The best response to a suspicious "bank" message is to...

options.label: Contact the bank through its official number or website
Reply to the message to verify

questions.prompt: A credit freeze...

options.label: Blocks new accounts in your name — and it's free

lessons.title: Assets vs. Liabilities
lessons.conceptMarkdown:
## Assets vs. Liabilities

**Net worth = what you own − what you owe.**

- **Assets:** cash, savings, investments, retirement accounts, home equity — things that hold or grow value.
- **Liabilities:** credit card balances, student/auto loans, money owed to anyone.

Income is *not* wealth. A $200k earner spending $210k has negative net worth; a $60k earner investing $10k/year quietly passes them in a decade. Wealth is what's *kept*, not what's earned.

Every financial decision in this course ultimately does one of two things: **builds an asset or shrinks a liability.** That's the whole game.

questions.prompt: Net worth equals...
A high salary guarantees...

options.label: Nothing about net worth without spending habits

lessons.title: Tracking Progress
lessons.conceptMarkdown:
## Tracking Progress

Compute net worth **once or twice a year**:

1. List every asset and its value
2. List every debt and its balance
3. Subtract. That number is your net worth.

The **trend matters more than the number** — a graph climbing from −$8k to +$5k over two years is a bigger win than a flat $50k.

Then automate the trend: payday transfers to savings (Unit 2), auto-investing (Unit 12), auto-payments on debts (Unit 7). Progress you don't have to remember is progress that actually happens — willpower schedules, automation keeps.

questions.prompt: How often should you check your net worth?

options.label: Once or twice a year — the trend matters

questions.prompt: The best lens for any money decision is...

options.label: Does this build an asset or shrink a liability?

lessons.title: Your Simple Plan
lessons.conceptMarkdown:
## Your Simple Plan

The entire course, in order:

1. **Budget** — 50/30/20, savings moved on payday
2. **Starter emergency fund** — $500–$1,000
3. **Employer match** — capture it fully (free 50–100%)
4. **Kill high-interest debt** — 24% APR beats 7% returns
5. **Full emergency fund** — 3–6 months of essentials
6. **Invest automatically** — low-cost index funds, every month
7. **Protect** — insurance for catastrophes, 2FA everywhere
8. **Repeat for decades** — compounding does the rest

The order matters: a 24% debt is a guaranteed 24% "return" when paid off; no investment reliably beats that. And **automation beats willpower** — set the flows once, then live your life.

questions.prompt: Before investing in index funds, you should typically...

options.label: Kill high-interest debt and build the emergency fund

questions.prompt: Why automate the plan?

options.label: Willpower fails; automation makes good choices the default

lessons.title: The Long Game
lessons.conceptMarkdown:
## The Long Game

**Financial independence** is the point where your investments can cover your living costs — work becomes a choice. Every dollar invested shortens that timeline; every dollar of lifestyle inflation extends it.

What actually gets people there is not brilliance. It's **boring consistency**: an automatic monthly transfer into index funds, sustained for decades, through crashes and headlines.

Revisit the plan once a year — income changes, goals change, the *order* never does.

You now hold the fundamentals most people never learn: spend less than you earn, protect yourself, invest the difference, and let time do the heavy lifting. **This is educational content, not financial advice — but it's a very good place to start.**

questions.prompt: "Financial independence" means...

options.label: Your investments can cover your living expenses
You never work again under any circumstances
